Explain the terms: channel, Vth, triode, saturation, short-channel effects

How a MOSFET turns on, step by step

  1. Off: with no gate voltage the body’s majority carriers (holes in an NMOS) sit right under the oxide. The source and drain are separated by two back-to-back PN junctions, so nothing flows.
  2. Depletion: a small positive gate voltage pushes the holes away. Fixed, charged dopant ions are left behind. They cannot move, so there is still no current.
  3. Inversion: above the threshold voltage Vth, the gate pulls in enough electrons to form a thin n-type layer under the oxide: the channel. It now connects source and drain.
  4. Linear (triode): a small VDS makes electrons drift through the channel. The device behaves like a resistor whose value the gate sets.
  5. Saturation: once VDS ≥ VGS − Vth, the channel pinches off at the drain end. Extra VDS mostly drops across the drain depletion region, so the current levels off.

Conditions with your current settings:

Why the current stops growing in saturation

The gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end is VGS − VDS. When that falls to Vth, the drain end of the channel can hold no more carriers: it pinches off. Carriers that reach the pinch-off point are swept across the strong field of the drain depletion region, so the current is set by how many carriers the channel can supply, ½k(VGS − Vth)², not by VDS.

Device terms

Source / Drain
Heavily doped regions (n+ or p+) where carriers enter and leave the channel.
Gate
Electrode on top of a thin oxide. Its voltage attracts or repels carriers below it; no DC current flows into it.
Body
The substrate or well the transistor sits in. Usually tied to the source.
Oxide
Thin insulating SiO₂ (or high-k) layer between gate and silicon.
Majority carrier
The carrier the body is doped with: holes in p-type, electrons in n-type.
Depletion region
A zone emptied of mobile carriers, leaving fixed ions.
Fixed ion
An ionised dopant atom locked in the crystal: acceptors are −, donors are +.
Inversion
The surface switches type (p → n for NMOS) because the gate attracted enough minority carriers.
Vth
Threshold voltage: the VGS where inversion starts and a channel forms.
VOV
Overdrive, VGS − Vth: how far above threshold the gate is.
k = μCox·W/L
Transconductance parameter: mobility × oxide capacitance × width/length. Sets how much current the device gives.
Pinch-off
The point where the channel thickness reaches zero at the drain end.

Short-channel effects

CLM (λ)
Channel-length modulation: the pinch-off point moves toward the source as VDS rises, so ID still grows a little in saturation.
DIBL
Drain-induced barrier lowering: in a short channel the drain field lowers the source barrier, so Vth drops as VDS rises.
Velocity saturation
Carriers have a top speed (~10⁷ cm/s). Short channels reach it, so current saturates early and grows only linearly with VGS.
Body effect
Reverse body bias widens depletion and raises Vth. See the Body effect tab.

Transfer curve and supply current

What is happening

Explain the terms: VTC, switching point, regions A–E, power

How a CMOS inverter works

  1. The PMOS connects the output to VDD, the NMOS connects it to ground. Both gates share the input.
  2. Input low: the NMOS is off and the PMOS is on, so the output is pulled up to VDD (logic 1).
  3. Input high: the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on, so the output is pulled down to 0 V (logic 0).
  4. Only one transistor is on in each steady state, so almost no current flows. Current flows only briefly while switching, when both are partly on.

The five regions of the transfer curve

The switching point VM is where Vout = VDD/2. It sits where the NMOS and PMOS are equally strong. Holes are slower than electrons, so with equal widths the PMOS loses and VM moves below VDD/2. Making the PMOS about 2.5× wider balances them and gives equal noise margins for 0 and 1.

Where the power goes

Static power is almost zero. Dynamic power is spent charging and discharging the load capacitance each time the output switches: P = α·C·VDD²·f. That is why lowering VDD (see DVFS in the Power tab) saves so much energy.

Inverter terms

VTC
Voltage transfer curve: Vout plotted against Vin.
VM
Switching threshold: the input where Vout = Vin = VDD/2.
Noise margin
How much noise an input can carry and still be read correctly (NML for logic 0, NMH for logic 1).
Pull-up / pull-down
The PMOS pulls the output up to VDD; the NMOS pulls it down to ground.
Through current
Also called short-circuit current: flows from VDD to ground only while both transistors are partly on.
Wp/Wn
Width ratio. A wider PMOS compensates for slower holes.
kn, kp
Strength of each transistor: μCox·W/L.
Rail-to-rail
The output swings all the way from 0 V to VDD.
Gain region
Region C, where both devices are saturated and a small Vin change gives a large Vout change.
Dynamic power
α·C·VDD²·f: energy spent charging the output capacitance every switching event.

Response and threshold shift

Why the body effect appears here

Explain the terms: body effect, VSB, γ, stacks, weak 1

What the body effect is

  1. Every MOSFET has a fourth terminal, the body (substrate or well). In digital circuits it is tied to ground (NMOS) or VDD (PMOS).
  2. If the source rises above the body, the source-body junction is reverse-biased by VSB.
  3. That reverse bias widens the depletion layer under the gate, so it holds more fixed charge.
  4. The gate must now overcome that extra charge before it can form a channel, so the threshold voltage rises: Vth = Vth0 + γ(√(2φF + VSB) − √2φF).

Right now:

How designers live with it

  • In a NAND/NOR stack, put the latest-arriving (critical) input on the transistor closest to the output, so the slow-to-settle middle node is already charged.
  • Keep stacks short (2–3 transistors) and size the stacked devices wider.
  • Use a transmission gate (NMOS + PMOS) instead of a single pass transistor, so a full 0 and 1 are passed.
  • In analog circuits, put the transistor in its own well (or a deep n-well / triple-well process) and tie body to source, which removes the effect.

Terms

Body / bulk
The silicon the transistor is built in: p-substrate for NMOS, n-well for PMOS.
VSB / VBS
Source-to-body voltage (NMOS) or body-to-source voltage (PMOS). Positive means reverse bias.
γ (gamma)
Body-effect coefficient, √(2qεNA)/Cox. Higher doping or thicker oxide gives a bigger γ.
2φF
Surface potential at strong inversion, about 0.6–0.8 V depending on doping.
Stack
Transistors in series. Only the bottom one has its source on the rail.
Node X / Y
The internal node between two stacked transistors. Its voltage is the VSB of the upper device.
Weak 1
An NMOS can only pass up to VDD − Vth(raised): about 1.9 V instead of 3.3 V here.
Transmission gate
NMOS and PMOS in parallel: the PMOS passes the high level the NMOS cannot.
Source follower
Amplifier whose output (source) follows its input (gate) one VGS lower.
gm, gmb
Gate and body transconductance. gmb = η·gm acts against gm in a follower.
η
γ / (2√(2φF + VSB)): body-effect factor, usually 0.1–0.3.
Level shift
The DC drop Vin − Vout of a follower: Vth + VOV.

Explain the terms: LDO, dropout, buck, duty cycle, PMIC, DVFS

Two ways to make a lower voltage

LDO (linear)Buck (switching)
HowA PMOS acts as a variable resistor and drops the extra voltageSwitches chop Vin; an L–C filter averages it to D·Vin
Efficiency≈ Vout/Vin (poor for a big drop)≈ 85–95 %, almost independent of the drop
Output noiseVery clean, rejects input rippleSwitching ripple at f and its harmonics

With your current settings:

How the output voltage is changed (modulated)

  1. LDO: Vout = Vref·(1 + R1/R2). Change the divider ratio or the reference voltage.
  2. Buck: Vout ≈ D·Vin. The controller changes the duty cycle D: the PWM comparator keeps the high side on until the ramp crosses the error-amplifier output.
  3. PMIC: the processor writes a VSEL code over I²C/SPMI. A DAC turns the code into a new reference, and the regulator’s loop moves the output there at a controlled slew rate.

Why it matters: a processor’s dynamic power is P = α·C·V²·f. Dropping the core from 1.05 V to 0.60 V at idle cuts that power by about 3×, which is the whole point of DVFS.

LDO terms

LDO
Low-dropout linear regulator: works with Vin only slightly above Vout.
Pass device
The large PMOS between input and output that carries the load current.
Error amplifier
Compares the divided output (FB) with Vref and drives the pass-device gate.
Vref
A precise internal reference voltage (0.8 V here), often from a bandgap circuit.
Dropout
Minimum Vin − Vout for regulation. Below it the output just follows Vin.
Load / line regulation
How much Vout changes when the load current / input voltage changes.
PSRR
Power-supply rejection: how well input ripple is kept out of the output.
Load transient
The dip or overshoot of Vout when the load current jumps, before the loop catches up.

Switching and PMIC terms

Buck
Step-down switching converter.
Duty cycle D
Fraction of the period the high-side switch is on.
PWM
Pulse-width modulation: the control method that sets D.
SW node
The switch node between the two transistors; a square wave between Vin and 0 V.
High / low side
The switch to Vin (PMOS here) and the switch to ground (NMOS here).
ΔiL
Inductor ripple current: (Vin − Vout)·D/(f·L).
CCM / DCM
Continuous / discontinuous conduction: whether the inductor current stays above zero.
PMIC
Power-management IC: several regulators, references and control logic in one chip.
Rail
One supply output (e.g. CPU core, I/O, analog).
DVFS
Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: lower V and f when the load is light.
VSEL
Register that selects the output voltage of a regulator.
Slew rate
Speed of a voltage change, e.g. 10 mV/µs.

Spectrum and trade-offs

How it works

Explain the terms: Rmax, beat frequency, “no peak”, PLL words

How the radar turns distance into a tone

  1. The radar sends a chirp: a signal whose frequency rises steadily, e.g. 76 → 77 GHz in 40 µs.
  2. The echo comes back a little later, so at every moment it is at a slightly lower frequency than what is being sent.
  3. Mixing the echo with the transmit signal leaves the difference: a tone called the beat frequency fb. The farther the target, the longer the delay and the higher the tone: fb = 2·R·S / c.
  4. The receiver filter and ADC only pass tones up to the IF bandwidth (20 MHz here). The distance whose tone just reaches that limit is Rmax.

With your current settings:

What “no peak” means

No peak means the radar cannot detect that target with the current chirp settings. The car is still there, but its tone is above the receiver bandwidth, so it is filtered out before the FFT ever sees it. It is not a fault: it is the limit of that chirp design.

Why a larger bandwidth B shortens Rmax

Sweeping more bandwidth in the same time makes the chirp steeper, so every target’s tone is higher and the 20 MHz limit is reached at a shorter distance. Same 60 m car:

This is the basic trade-off: large B gives fine detail (ΔR = c/2B, 3.75 cm at 4 GHz) but a steep chirp gives short reach. Real ADAS radars switch between modes:

ModeTypical chirpReachDetailUse
Long rangeB ≈ 0.3–1 GHz, long Tc≈ 200–250 m15–50 cmHighway, adaptive cruise
Medium rangeB ≈ 1–2 GHz≈ 60–100 m7–15 cmCity traffic, cut-in
Short rangeB up to 4 GHz≈ 20–30 m≈ 4 cmParking, blind spot

Rmax in this demo is only the limit set by the receiver bandwidth. A real radar has a second limit: echo strength falls roughly as 1/R⁴, so a far or small target (a pedestrian instead of a truck) can be too weak to rise above the noise. That limit is not modelled here.

FMCW terms

Chirp
A signal whose frequency rises linearly with time.
B
Chirp bandwidth: how far the frequency sweeps (e.g. 1 GHz).
Tc
Chirp duration: how long one sweep lasts.
S
Slope, S = B/Tc: how fast it sweeps (MHz per µs).
τ
Round-trip delay, τ = 2R/c (400 ns for 60 m).
fb / IF
Beat (intermediate) frequency after the mixer, fb = S·τ. It encodes distance.
IF bandwidth
Highest beat frequency the filter and ADC pass (20 MHz here).
Rmax
Farthest distance whose tone fits in the IF bandwidth: fIF,max·c/(2S).
FFT peak
The FFT finds which tones are present. Each peak is one target; its position gives the distance.
ΔR
Range resolution, c/2B: two targets closer than this merge into one peak.
Doppler
A moving target shifts the echo phase a little from chirp to chirp; that rate gives its speed (fd = 2v/λ).
λ
Wavelength, about 3.9 mm at 77 GHz.

PLL / synthesizer terms

XO / fref
Crystal oscillator: a very stable, low-frequency reference (e.g. 50 MHz).
VCO
Voltage-controlled oscillator: its frequency follows the tuning voltage Vtune.
Varactor
A MOS capacitor whose capacitance changes with voltage (accumulation = high C, depletion = low C). It tunes the VCO.
÷N
Divider: brings the VCO down to fref so it can be compared. Fractional N allows any frequency, not just multiples of fref.
ΣΔ
Sigma-delta modulator: switches the divider between N and N+1 so the average equals the fractional N.
PFD / CP / LF
Phase-frequency detector, charge pump and loop filter: measure the phase error and turn it into a smooth Vtune.
Loop BW
How fast the loop reacts. Wider tracks the chirp better and cleans VCO noise; narrower filters reference and ΣΔ noise.
Phase noise
Random jitter of the carrier phase, in dBc/Hz at an offset frequency. It raises the noise floor around every FFT peak.
×4
Frequency multiplier: 19–20 GHz VCO → 76–81 GHz output (phase noise rises by 20·log4 = 12 dB).

Equations

Response and S-parameters

How it works

Explain the terms: S-parameters, Smith chart, coupler, balun, antenna, TE / TM modes

How to read S-parameters

  1. Each port of a component is fed from a line with a reference impedance Z0, usually 50 Ω. Power travels in as a wave a and comes back out as a wave b.
  2. Sij is the wave leaving port i when only port j is driven: S11 is the reflection at port 1, S21 the transmission from port 1 to port 2.
  3. They are complex numbers: the magnitude (usually in dB) says how much comes out, the angle says how much it is delayed.
  4. A passive, lossless component keeps the power: |S11|² + |S21|² + … = 1 for each driven port. Whatever is not reflected or passed on is turned into heat or radiated.

With your current settings:

Return loss, VSWR and mismatch

|S11|Return lossVSWRPower reflected
−6 dB6 dB3.025 %
−10 dB10 dB1.9210 %
−15 dB15 dB1.433.2 %
−20 dB20 dB1.221 %

A common target is |S11| below −10 dB across the band: only 10 % of the power is reflected.

TE, TM and TEM

In a TE mode the electric field is purely transverse (Ez = 0) and the magnetic field has a component along the guide. In a TM mode it is the other way round (Hz = 0). A TEM wave has neither Ez nor Hz; it needs two conductors (coax, microstrip, a pair of wires) and has no cutoff. A hollow metal pipe has only one conductor, so it carries only TE and TM modes, and each mode propagates only above its cutoff frequency.

Network terms

Z0
Reference (characteristic) impedance of the ports, 50 Ω here.
Γ = S11
Reflection coefficient: (Z − Z0)/(Z + Z0). 0 means matched, 1 means everything bounces back.
Return loss
−20·log|S11|. Bigger is better.
Insertion loss
−20·log|S21|: how much weaker the signal is after passing through.
VSWR
Ratio of the maximum to the minimum of the standing wave, (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|).
Smith chart
A map of Γ. The centre is a perfect match; circles are constant resistance, arcs constant reactance.
λ/4 transformer
A quarter-wave line of Zl = √(Z1·Z2) matches Z1 to Z2.

Component terms

Directional coupler
Four-port that taps a fixed fraction of a wave travelling one way, e.g. to measure the forward power of a PA.
Coupling / isolation
Coupling: input to coupled port. Isolation: input to the port that should get nothing.
Directivity
Isolation minus coupling: how well the coupler tells forward from reflected waves.
Even / odd mode
The two ways a pair of coupled lines can be driven (in phase / opposite). Their impedances Z0e and Z0o set the coupling.
Hybrid
A 3 dB coupler: two equal outputs, 90° (quadrature) or 180° apart.
Balun
BALanced–UNbalanced: turns a single-ended signal into two equal, opposite (differential) signals and back.
Amplitude / phase imbalance
How far the two balun outputs are from equal size and exactly 180° apart.
CMRR
Common-mode rejection: differential output compared with the leftover in-phase part.
Dipole
Two straight wires fed in the middle. Resonant when about half a wavelength long.
Radiation resistance
The part of the antenna's input resistance that stands for power radiated away (73 Ω for a half-wave dipole).
Directivity (dBi)
How much stronger the antenna radiates in its best direction than an ideal isotropic antenna.
E-plane pattern
Radiation versus angle in the plane that contains the dipole; nulls are along the wire.
Low-pass / high-pass
A filter that passes frequencies below / above its cutoff and blocks the rest. A lossless LC filter blocks by reflecting the power back, not by burning it.
Filter order N
Number of L and C elements. Each one adds 20 dB per decade (6 dB per octave) to the slope outside the passband.
Butterworth / Chebyshev
Butterworth is maximally flat in the passband; Chebyshev allows a small ripple (0.5 dB here) in exchange for a steeper edge.
Stepped-impedance filter
A low-pass filter made only of line sections: short, narrow high-Z lines act like series inductors and short, wide low-Z lines like shunt capacitors.
Richards' transformation
A short-circuited stub of length λ/8 at fc has jX = jZs·tan(βl), which behaves like an inductor; an open stub behaves like a capacitor.
Coaxial cavity low-pass
A metal tube with a centre rod: thin rod sections (high Z) act as series L, wide discs (low Z) as shunt C. Air-filled, so very low loss and high power.
Waveguide high-pass
A hollow guide passes nothing below the cutoff of its TE10 mode, fc = c/2a. Below it the field decays as e^(−αz), so the guide itself is the filter.
Band-pass filter
Passes a band around f0 and blocks both sides. Made from resonators tuned to f0 whose couplings set the bandwidth.
Coupled-cavity filter
A chain of metal resonant cavities joined by irises. Each coupling k(i,i+1) and the external Q at the ends follow from the prototype g values.
Unloaded Q (Qu)
Loss of a single resonator. The passband loss is about 4.343·Σg / (Δ·Qu) dB, so narrow filters need high-Q cavities.
Spurious passband
Line lengths repeat every half wavelength, so a transmission-line filter's response comes back at higher frequencies.
Group delay
How long the signal envelope takes to pass, −dφ/dω. It peaks near the cutoff, where the filter rings most.
Cutoff fc
Lowest frequency at which a waveguide mode propagates. Below it the field dies out (evanescent).
Dominant mode
The mode with the lowest cutoff, TE10 in a rectangular guide.
λg, vp, vg
Guide wavelength, phase velocity (faster than light) and group velocity (the speed of energy, slower than light).

Patterns and trade-offs

How it works

Explain the terms: phased array, beam switching, MIMO, virtual array, car radar layouts

From one antenna to a steerable beam

  1. Every antenna element sends out the same wave. Far away the waves add up, and the result depends on the direction.
  2. If all elements are in phase, the waves add best straight ahead (broadside): the main beam.
  3. Delay each element a little more than its neighbour, by Δφ = −k·d·sinθ0, and the waves now line up in the direction θ0: the beam is steered without moving anything.
  4. Beam switching picks one of a few fixed beams instead of setting any angle; MIMO uses several transmitters and receivers to build a much larger virtual array in software.

With your current settings:

Steering vs switching vs MIMO

Phased arraySwitched beamsMIMO (digital)
How the beam is formedPhase shifter on every elementFixed network (Butler matrix) + switchFFT over the virtual array after the ADC
Beam directionsAny angle (set by bits)M fixed anglesAll angles at once
LossPhase-shifter loss, quantisation lobesCrossover loss between beamsNone in the beam, but more data
SpeedFast (ns to µs per beam)Sweep time = M × dwellOne frame sees every angle
Typical use5G mmWave, satellite, military radarLow-cost 60 GHz links, simple radars77 GHz car radar

Array terms

Array factor AF(θ)
The sum of all element signals in direction θ, Σ wn·e^(j·n·k·d·sinθ). The beam pattern is |AF|².
Broadside / endfire
Broadside is straight out of the array (θ = 0); endfire is along the array (θ = ±90°).
Beamwidth (HPBW)
Angle between the −3 dB points, about 0.886·λ / (N·d·cosθ0) radians for a uniform array.
Array gain
N elements add coherently: 10·log N dB more than one element.
Sidelobe
Smaller beams beside the main one (−13 dB for uniform weights). A taper lowers them but widens the main beam.
Grating lobe
A second full-size beam that appears when d > λ / (1 + |sinθ0|). Keep d ≤ λ/2 to scan anywhere.
Phase quantisation
A b-bit phase shifter only sets 2^b phases; the rounding error raises sidelobes and shifts the beam slightly.
Scan loss
The beam gets wider and the element gain drops as θ0 moves away from broadside.

MIMO and car terms

Butler matrix
A passive network of hybrids and fixed phase shifters: N inputs, N outputs, each input gives one fixed beam.
Crossover loss
Gain lost when the target sits between two switched beams (about 3.9 dB for touching DFT beams).
Virtual array
Every TX–RX pair acts as one element at position x_tx + x_rx, so Ntx × Nrx channels come from only Ntx + Nrx antennas.
TDM / DDM-MIMO
Ways to separate the transmitters: one after another in time, or with different Doppler (phase) codes at the same time.
Angular resolution
Smallest angle between two targets that still shows two peaks, about 2/Nv radians for λ/2 spacing.
Cascaded radar
Several radar chips (e.g. 4 × 3TX/4RX) sharing one clock (LO) to act as one big MIMO radar: an "imaging radar".
Corner radar
Short-range radar at a car corner, wide field of view, for blind spot, lane change and cross traffic.

Equations

Output characteristics

How it works

Explain the terms: current mirror, diode connection, output resistance, compliance, cascode, matching

How a current mirror copies a current

  1. M1 is diode-connected: its gate is tied to its drain. Force Iref into it and it settles at exactly the VGS that carries Iref.
  2. M2 shares that gate voltage and the same source (ground). Same VGS, same Vth, same size → the same current.
  3. Make M2 wider and it carries more: Iout = (W2/W1)·Iref. This is how one reference feeds many bias currents on a chip.
  4. It only works while M2 stays in saturation (Vout ≥ VGS − Vth). Below that it falls into triode and the current drops.
  5. In saturation the current still rises a little with Vout (channel-length modulation), so the mirror is not a perfect current source: its output resistance is ro = 1/(λ·Iout).

With your current settings:

Mirror types

TypeOutput resistanceMinimum VoutNotes
Basic (2 transistors)roVov ≈ 0.2–0.5 VSimple; output current depends on Vout

Terms

Current mirror
A circuit that copies a reference current to one or more outputs, scaled by transistor size.
Diode-connected
Gate tied to drain: VDS = VGS, so the transistor is always in saturation and behaves like a resistor of about 1/gm.
Mirror ratio
Iout/Iref = (W2/L2)/(W1/L1). Ratios are made from whole unit transistors for good matching.
Output resistance
ΔVout/ΔIout. Infinite for an ideal current source; ro for a single transistor.
λ (CLM)
Channel-length modulation, about λ0/L. Long transistors have smaller λ and higher ro.
Compliance (headroom)
Lowest output voltage at which the mirror still delivers its current.
Vov
Overdrive VGS − Vth. Small Vov saves headroom but makes the current more sensitive to Vth mismatch.
Cascode
A second transistor stacked on the output that holds the bottom one's VDS constant, multiplying the output resistance by gm·ro.
Mismatch
Random differences between "identical" transistors: ΔI/I ≈ −2·ΔVth/Vov in saturation.
Pelgrom's law
σ(ΔVth) = AVT/√(W·L): bigger transistors match better.
Common centroid
Layout that interleaves the unit transistors so gradients across the chip cancel.
INL / DNL
Integral and differential non-linearity of a DAC, in LSB: how far each output, and each step, is from ideal.
PN

PN junction

Controls

p-side doping NA
n-side doping ND
Bias voltage V
Gate voltage VG
Oxide thickness tox
Substrate doping NA

Equations

Characteristics

How it works

Explain the terms: doping, band diagram, depletion, built-in voltage, breakdown, C-V

How a PN junction forms

  1. Pure silicon has very few free carriers (ni ≈ 10¹⁰ cm⁻³). Doping adds them: boron gives holes (p-type), phosphorus or arsenic gives electrons (n-type).
  2. Where p meets n, electrons diffuse into the p side and holes into the n side, and recombine.
  3. The dopant atoms they leave behind are charged and fixed: a depletion region with a strong electric field.
  4. The field pushes back on diffusion. Balance is reached at the built-in voltage Vbi ≈ 0.6–0.9 V.
  5. An external voltage tips the balance: forward lowers the barrier (current e^(V/Vt)), reverse raises it (only leakage, until breakdown).

Your doping at a few bias points:

How to read a band diagram

Up means higher electron energy. Electrons live on or above Ec and roll downhill; holes live on or below Ev and float uphill. A sloped band means an electric field. The Fermi level EF marks how full the states are: close to Ec means n-type, close to Ev means p-type. In equilibrium EF is flat everywhere; an applied voltage V splits it by qV.

Where these junctions appear on this site

PlaceJunctionWhy it matters
Every MOSFETSource/drain to body (reverse biased)Isolates transistors; leakage and capacitance
Body effect tabSource-body reverse bias VSBWider depletion raises Vth
77 GHz VCOMOS varactor (this C-V curve)Tuning voltage sets capacitance and frequency
ESD protectionDiodes to the supply railsSteer surge current away from the gates
Image sensors, solar cellsPhotodiodeLight makes electron-hole pairs in the depletion region

Junction terms

ni
Intrinsic carrier density of pure silicon, about 10¹⁰ cm⁻³ at room temperature.
Acceptor / donor
Dopant that takes an electron (boron → hole, p-type) or gives one (phosphorus → electron, n-type).
Ec, Ev, Eg
Conduction-band edge, valence-band edge and the band gap between them (1.12 eV in silicon).
Fermi level EF
Energy at which a state is half likely to be filled; it tells how n- or p-type the material is.
Vt = kT/q
Thermal voltage, 25.9 mV at 300 K: the natural voltage scale of carrier statistics.
Diffusion / drift
Carriers move from high to low concentration (diffusion) or are pushed by an electric field (drift).
Minority injection
In forward bias electrons enter the p side and holes the n side, where they are the minority and recombine.
Is
Reverse saturation current: tiny, set by ni², doping and diffusion lengths; doubles roughly every 5–6 °C.
Avalanche
Carriers gain enough energy in the field to knock out new electron-hole pairs, which multiply.
Zener breakdown
In very heavily doped junctions electrons tunnel straight through the thin barrier (below about 5 V).

MOS capacitor terms

Accumulation
Majority carriers (holes) gather at the surface; C ≈ Cox.
Depletion
Holes are pushed away; fixed charge forms a layer that grows with VG and lowers C.
Inversion
The surface holds more electrons than the bulk holds holes: it acts as n-type.
ψs
Surface potential: total band bending at the oxide interface.
φF
Fermi potential: (kT/q)·ln(NA/ni); strong inversion starts at ψs = 2φF.
VFB
Flat-band voltage: gate voltage that makes the bands flat (set by the work-function difference and oxide charge).
Cox
Oxide capacitance per area, εox/tox.
LF / HF C-V
At low frequency the inversion electrons follow the signal (C back to Cox); at high frequency they cannot, so C stays at its minimum.
Varactor
A voltage-controlled capacitor built from this structure; it tunes oscillators such as the radar VCO.
SUB

Subthreshold leakage

Controls

Gate length L
Body thickness tsi
Gate voltage VGS
Drain voltage VDS
Temperature T

Equations

Characteristics

How it works

Explain the terms: subthreshold swing, Ion/Ioff, DIBL, Vth flavours, FinFET, GAA

Why a transistor never turns fully off

  1. Electrons in the source have a spread of thermal energies. Their number falls by 10× for every 60 meV of extra energy at room temperature (the Boltzmann tail).
  2. The gate controls an energy barrier between source and drain. Only electrons above the barrier get through.
  3. Each 60 mV the gate raises the barrier (at best) removes 90 % of the current. So below Vth, current falls exponentially, but never to zero.
  4. To keep leakage small, Vth cannot go much below ~0.25–0.3 V, so VDD cannot go much below ~0.6–0.7 V. This "Boltzmann tyranny" is why supply voltages stopped shrinking.

Your transistor:

How the industry fought leakage

Node (approx.)StructureKey change
90–45 nmPlanar, strained SiFaster carriers; high-k metal gate at 45 nm cuts gate leakage
28–20 nmPlanar (and FD-SOI)Last planar nodes; thin-body SOI as an alternative
22/16 nm – 5/4 nmFinFETGate on 3 sides of a thin fin
3/2 nm and beyondGAA nanosheetGate on all 4 sides; sheet width sets drive
FutureCFET, 2D materialsStack n and p devices; atom-thin channels

Node names like "3 nm" are marketing labels today; the real gate length is closer to 12–16 nm. What matters is how well the gate wraps the channel relative to its length (L/λ).

Leakage terms

Subthreshold swing SS
Gate voltage per decade of current below Vth; 60 mV/dec at 300 K is the physical limit.
Ion / Ioff
On current (speed) and off current (standby leakage) per µm of width.
Body factor n
1 + Cdep/Cox: the fraction of gate voltage lost to the depletion capacitance. Thin, fully depleted bodies get close to 1.
DIBL
Drain-induced barrier lowering: the drain voltage reduces Vth (mV per V).
LVT / SVT / HVT
Low, standard and high threshold transistors offered by the same process; designers mix them to trade speed for leakage.
GIDL
Gate-induced drain leakage: band-to-band tunnelling at the drain edge when the gate is strongly off.
Gate leakage
Electrons tunnelling through a very thin oxide; solved by high-k dielectrics (HfO₂) with a thicker physical layer.
Junction leakage
Reverse-biased source/drain diode current (see the PN junction tab).
Power gating
Switching whole blocks off with a high-Vth header or footer transistor to stop their leakage.

Structure terms

Scale length λ
Decay length of the gate's influence into the body; good control needs L ≳ 5λ.
FinFET
Channel stood up as a thin vertical fin, gate wrapped over three sides.
GAA / nanosheet
Gate-all-around: stacked horizontal sheets, each fully surrounded by the gate.
Fin / sheet pitch
Spacing between fins or stacks; sets how much width fits per unit area.
Effective width
Total gated channel perimeter; fins and stacked sheets give more of it per footprint.
Fully depleted
A body so thin that it is entirely depleted, which improves n and SS.
EOT
Equivalent oxide thickness: high-k layer expressed as the SiO₂ thickness with the same capacitance.

How it works

Explain the terms: SRAM, DRAM, flash, SNM, refresh, charge sharing, ISPP, MLC

Three ways to store a bit

SRAMDRAMFlash
Bit stored asState of a latch (2 inverters)Charge on a capacitorElectrons on a floating gate
Transistors per bit61 (+1 capacitor)1 (or ⅓ with TLC)
Keeps data without power?NoNo (and leaks within ms)Yes, for years

Your settings:

All three are built from the same MOSFET. SRAM uses it as a switch, DRAM as a valve for charge, and flash adds a second, floating gate that turns the threshold voltage itself into the stored value.

SRAM terms

Word line (WL)
Row signal that opens the access transistors of every cell in the row.
Bit lines (BL, BLB)
Column wires that carry the data in and out, as a complementary pair.
Precharge
Charging the bit lines to a known voltage before a read.
Sense amplifier
Fast latch that turns a small bit-line difference into a full logic level.
SNM
Static noise margin: size of the largest square in the butterfly plot's eye.
Read disturb
The 0 node is pulled up during a read; too much and the cell flips.
Cell ratio β
Pull-down / access strength; sets read stability.

DRAM and flash terms

Charge sharing
Cell and bit line settle to a common voltage; the bit line moves only by Cs/(Cs + Cbl) of the difference.
Refresh
Periodic read-and-rewrite of every row before its charge leaks away.
Retention time
How long a stored value survives without refresh (DRAM) or power (flash).
Floating gate / charge trap
Isolated storage layer for electrons; modern 3D NAND uses a silicon-nitride charge-trap layer instead.
Fowler-Nordheim tunnelling
Electrons tunnelling through a thin oxide under a very high field.
ISPP
Incremental step pulse programming: pulse, verify, pulse a bit higher.
SLC / MLC / TLC / QLC
1, 2, 3 or 4 bits per cell = 2, 4, 8 or 16 Vth levels.
Endurance
Number of program/erase cycles before the cell becomes unreliable.
ECC
Error-correcting code that repairs bits whose Vth drifted across a read reference.
3D NAND
Cells stacked in 100–300 layers around vertical channels.

Receiver chain and noise

Controls

Target range R
LNA gain

IF gain
High-pass corner
Resolution N
Input voltage Vin

Equations

Performance

How it works

Explain the terms: radar equation, noise figure, Friis, LNA, mixer, IF, ADC, SQNR

The receive path, step by step

  1. Antenna: collects the echo, often less than a picowatt.
  2. LNA: amplifies it while adding as little noise as possible (optional at 77 GHz in CMOS).
  3. Mixer: multiplies it by the transmit chirp (LO) and produces the beat frequency fb, a few MHz.
  4. IF filter and amplifier: high-pass for leakage and near/far balance, low-pass against aliasing.
  5. ADC: samples the beat signal, typically 12 bits at 20–50 MS/s.
  6. FFT and detection: each target becomes a peak; peaks above the noise by about 13 dB count as detections.

Detection range with your receiver:

The radar now has two range limits: the IF bandwidth (fb must stay below 20 MHz, see the radar tab) and the echo power (SNR must stay above the threshold). The shorter of the two wins.

Receiver terms

Radar equation
Pr = Pt·G²·λ²·σ/((4π)³R⁴): echo power for a target with radar cross-section σ.
RCS σ
Radar cross-section: how big a target looks to the radar (car ≈ 10 m², pedestrian ≈ 0.5 m²).
kT
Thermal noise power density: −174 dBm per Hz at room temperature.
Noise figure NF
How many dB a stage worsens the signal-to-noise ratio.
Friis formula
Total noise factor; later stages count less because of the gain in front of them.
LNA
Low-noise amplifier: first gain stage, sets most of the noise figure.
LO
Local oscillator: the chirp from the PLL, used to mix the echo down.
IF
Intermediate frequency: the beat signal after the mixer.
Processing gain
SNR gained by the FFT (noise bandwidth 1/Tc) and by adding chirps coherently.

ADC terms

SAR
Successive approximation register: finds the code by binary search.
Capacitive DAC
Binary-weighted capacitors that produce each trial voltage.
Comparator
Decides whether the input is above or below the trial level.
LSB
Least significant bit: the smallest step, Vref/2^N.
SQNR / ENOB
Quantisation-limited SNR, 6.02N + 1.76 dB; ENOB is the effective number of bits including real noise.
Sample rate
Must be at least twice the highest beat frequency (Nyquist).

Bipolar junction transistor

Equations

Characteristics

How it works

Explain the terms: emitter, base, collector, β, gm, Early effect, HBT, fT, fmax

How a bipolar transistor amplifies

  1. The emitter-base junction is forward biased: the emitter injects electrons into the base, e^(VBE/Vt) of them.
  2. The base is so thin that almost all of them reach the far side before recombining.
  3. The base-collector junction is reverse biased: its field sweeps them into the collector.
  4. The base only supplies holes for the few lost electrons, so a small IB controls a large IC = β·IB.

Your transistor:

BJT or MOSFET?

BJT / HBTMOSFET
Controlled byBase current (junction)Gate voltage (insulated)
Input currentIB = IC/βPractically zero
gm at the same currentIC/Vt (high)2·ID/Vov (3–10× lower)
Matching, 1/f noiseVery goodWorse
Density, logicPoorExcellent
Typical useRF front ends, precision analog, bandgapsDigital, memory, most analog

Bipolar terms

Emitter / base / collector
Injector, thin control layer and the region that collects the carriers.
Forward active
EB forward, BC reverse: the normal amplifying mode.
Saturation
Both junctions forward biased; used as a closed switch, slow to leave.
β (hFE)
Current gain IC/IB, typically 100–1000.
gm
Transconductance IC/Vt: 38.6 mS per mA at room temperature.
Early voltage VA
Measure of how much IC rises with VCE; output resistance ro = VA/IC.
Gummel plot
log IC and log IB against VBE; their gap is β.
Kirk effect
At high current the base effectively widens into the collector and fT drops.

High-frequency terms

HBT
Heterojunction bipolar transistor: base made of a different semiconductor (SiGe, InP).
Ge grading
Germanium content rising across the base; creates a built-in drift field.
τB, τF
Base transit time and total forward transit time of the carriers.
fT
Transit frequency: where the small-signal current gain drops to 1.
fmax
Maximum oscillation frequency: where power gain drops to 1.
BiCMOS
Process with both bipolar transistors and CMOS on one chip.
BGR

Bandgap voltage reference

Controls

Temperature T
Area ratio N
Resistor ratio K = R2/R1
Input difference Vid
Tail current Iss
Compensation Cc

Equations

Characteristics

How it works

Explain the terms: PTAT, CTAT, bandgap, ppm/°C, differential pair, CMRR, GBW, phase margin

Why the bandgap works

  1. A forward-biased junction's voltage VBE drops by about 2 mV for every degree: CTAT.
  2. Two junctions at the same current but with different areas differ by ΔVBE = (kT/q)·ln N, which grows with temperature: PTAT.
  3. Add the PTAT term, scaled by K, to VBE. With the right K the slopes cancel.
  4. The result sits near 1.2 V, the band-gap voltage of silicon extrapolated to absolute zero.

Your reference:

The same PTAT current is also a free temperature sensor: on-chip thermometers measure ΔVBE, and the "temperature" readout of a phone or CPU usually comes from such a circuit.

Reference terms

CTAT / PTAT
Complementary / proportional to absolute temperature.
Band-gap voltage
About 1.2 V: VBE extrapolated to 0 K; the sum the circuit settles at.
ppm/°C
Drift in millionths of the output per degree; good references reach 1–10 ppm/°C.
Curvature
The remaining bow because VBE is not perfectly linear in T.
Trimming
Adjusting K (with fuses or registers) on every chip after test.
Start-up circuit
Extra circuit that kicks the bandgap out of its all-zero state at power-on.

Op-amp terms

Differential pair
Two matched transistors sharing a tail current; responds to the input difference.
CMRR
Common-mode rejection: how much better the amplifier responds to the difference than to the common level.
Active load
Current mirror used as the load; converts the two currents into one output.
GBW
Gain-bandwidth product: open-loop gain × bandwidth, constant for a one-pole amplifier.
Phase margin
180° minus the loop phase lag at unity gain; 45° rings, 60° is a good target.
Miller compensation
Capacitor across the second stage that splits the poles and sets GBW.
Slew rate
Fastest output change, Iss/Cc, when the input step fully switches the pair.
Offset
Input voltage needed to make the output zero, caused by mismatch of the pair.
LU

Controls

Trigger current
Substrate resistance Rsub
NMOS–well spacing
HBM voltage
Oxide breakdown

Equations

Characteristics

How it works

Explain the terms: latch-up, parasitic thyristor, guard ring, ESD, HBM, clamp

How latch-up starts and holds

  1. Every CMOS inverter hides a PNPN stack: p+ (PMOS) → n-well → p-substrate → n+ (NMOS).
  2. A disturbance injects current into the substrate; across Rsub it builds up 0.7 V.
  3. The parasitic NPN turns on and pulls current through the n-well resistance, which turns on the PNP.
  4. The PNP feeds the NPN's base: if βnpn·βpnp > 1, the loop keeps itself on after the trigger is gone.
  5. The chip draws a large current until it is powered down, or burns.

Your design:

The same junctions explain both pages: the PN-junction tab shows why a diode conducts at about 0.7 V, and the BJT tab shows the gain β that makes the parasitic loop dangerous.

Latch-up terms

Thyristor (SCR)
PNPN device that, once triggered, stays on until its current falls below the holding current.
Parasitic bipolar
Unintended transistor formed by the wells and diffusions of CMOS.
Well / substrate tap
Contact that ties the well to VDD or the substrate to GND; more taps = lower resistance.
Guard ring
Ring of tap diffusion around a device that collects stray carriers.
Holding voltage
Voltage the latched path settles at; if it is below VDD the latch persists.

ESD terms

ESD
Electrostatic discharge: a sudden current from a charged person, tool or device.
HBM / CDM
Human-body model (100 pF, 1.5 kΩ) and charged-device model (the chip itself discharges, < 1 ns).
Primary diodes
Diodes from each pin to VDD and VSS that steer ESD current to the rails.
Power clamp
Large NMOS between the rails, turned on by the fast ESD edge through an RC timer.
Oxide breakdown
Permanent short through the gate oxide when the field exceeds about 10 MV/cm.
ESD window
The protection must turn on above the normal operating voltage but below the breakdown of what it protects.

Every transistor on the other tabs is made this way. The PN junctions come from the implants, the gate oxide from oxidation, the MOS capacitor from gate + oxide + well, and the latch-up path from the wells and diffusions.

Process terms

Wafer
Thin disc of single-crystal silicon, today 300 mm in diameter.
Photoresist
Light-sensitive polymer; exposed areas dissolve in the developer (positive resist).

Lightly doped drain extension next to the gate, and a nitride wall that offsets the heavy source/drain implant.

Equations

Electrical and density

How it works

Explain the terms: back-grind, dicing, die attach, wire bond, RDL, UBM, bump, underfill, fan-out

From wafer to package

  1. Wafer test: every die is probed; bad ones are marked.
  2. Back-grind and dicing: the wafer is thinned and sawn into dies.
  3. Die attach: the die is glued (or soldered) to a lead frame or substrate.
  4. Interconnect: wire bonds, flip-chip bumps, or RDL in a fan-out package.
  5. Encapsulation: mold compound or underfill protects die and joints.
  6. Final test: electrical and RF test, burn-in for automotive parts, then tape and reel.

Assembly terms

Back-grinding
Thinning the wafer from the back side before dicing.
Scribe street
Empty lane between dies where the saw cuts.
Die attach
Bonding the die to the paddle or substrate with epoxy, film (DAF) or solder.
Free-air ball
Ball melted on the wire tip by an electric spark before the first bond.
Ball / stitch bond
First bond on the die pad, second bond on the lead.
Capillary
Ceramic tool that guides the wire and applies force and ultrasound.
EMC
Epoxy molding compound that encapsulates the die and wires.

Flip-chip and wafer-level terms

RDL
Redistribution layer: copper lines in polymer that move pads to new positions.
Passivation / PI
Nitride and polyimide layers that protect the chip and insulate the RDL.
UBM
Under-bump metallurgy: adhesion, barrier and wetting layers under the bump.
Bump / Cu pillar
Solder ball or copper post with a solder cap that forms the joint.
Reflow
Heating above the solder melting point; surface tension self-aligns the die.
Underfill
Epoxy under the flipped die that shares the thermal-expansion stress.
Fan-out
RDL extends beyond the die edge onto surrounding mold compound.
AiP
Antenna-in-package: radar antennas formed in the package RDL.
LiP

Waveguide (WR-12)
Hollow metal pipe, 3.10 × 1.55 mm inside, that carries 60–90 GHz in the TE10 mode with very low loss.
TSV / hybrid bonding
Through-silicon vias and direct copper-to-copper bonding for 3D stacking.

Equations

Analysis

What this signature suggests

How it works

Explain the terms: WAT, PCM, CP, bin map, D0, GDBN, PAT, DPPM

When yield is low where there is no WAT data

  1. Read the map: the shape of the failing area (edge, donut, center, line, repeat) points to the process step.
  2. Rule out the tester: per-site yield, probe card, touchdown pattern. A test problem is not a fab problem.
  3. Use data every die has: CP parametrics (ring oscillator, IDDQ, Vmin, RF gain, VCO frequency), calibrated against WAT where both exist.
  4. Use denser fab data: inline thickness and CD maps, defect inspection scans, tool and chamber history (commonality).
  5. Ask for more data: an engineering full-map WAT on the suspect wafers, nanoprobing and failure analysis on a failing die next to a good one.
  6. Design it in next time: your own monitors inside the die, so every die carries its own PCM.
  7. Protect the customer: GDBN, PAT and inking of the bad region until the cause is fixed.

SignatureLikely causeNext step

DonutPlasma or gas distribution, RTP lamp zonesChamber commonality, radial thickness / CD maps

Test terms

WAT
Wafer acceptance test: the fab's electrical test of test structures before the wafer ships.
PCM / testkey
Process control monitor: transistors, resistors, capacitors and chains placed in the scribe line.
Scribe line
The lane between dies that the dicing saw removes: free space for test structures.
CP / wafer sort
Circuit probe: every die is tested on the wafer with a probe card; results go into the bin map.
Bin
Test result category: pass, parametric fail, functional fail, contact fail.
Edge exclusion
Outer ring of the wafer (often 2–3 mm) that the fab does not guarantee.
Ring oscillator (RO)
Chain of inverters on the die whose frequency tracks transistor speed (Vth, Idsat).
IDDQ
Quiescent supply current: leakage of the whole die at rest; a defect often shows up as extra current.

Yield and screening terms

D0
Killer defect density per cm²: the main input of every yield model.
Kill ratio
Fraction of the defects of a type that actually make a die fail.
Commonality
Finding the tool, chamber or time that all bad lots share.
Nanoprobing
Landing fine probes on single transistors inside a die to measure Vth and Idsat directly.
EMMI / OBIRCH
Failure analysis methods that find leakage spots by emitted light or laser heating.
GDBN
Good die in bad neighbourhood: passing dies surrounded by failures are dropped.
PAT
Part average testing: outliers from the wafer's own distribution are dropped (AEC-Q001).
DPPM
Defective parts per million shipped: what the customer measures.
Latent defect
A defect that passes every test at time zero and fails later under voltage, current, heat or moisture.
Infant mortality
The early, falling part of the bathtub curve, caused mostly by latent defects.
Burn-in
Running chips hot (≈ 125 °C) at raised voltage for hours so weak ones fail in the factory.
Acceleration factor
How many hours of normal use one hour of stress is worth: AF = AF_T · AF_V.
TDDB
Time-dependent dielectric breakdown: traps build up in an oxide under field until it shorts.
Electromigration
Copper atoms pushed by the electron current; a narrowed line or via thins further until it opens.
HVST
High-voltage stress test: a short overvoltage step that breaks weak oxides during test.

WAT tells you the process was on target where it was measured. CP tells you every die. Use both: calibrate CP against WAT, then read the whole wafer.

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: NA, k1, σ, DOF, Bossung, LELE, SADP, SAQP, OPC, stochastics

How a pattern gets onto the wafer

  1. Coat: a thin photoresist film is spun onto the wafer and baked.
  2. Expose: the scanner images the mask (reticle) 4× reduced onto the wafer, one field at a time.
  3. Post-exposure bake: acid made by the light diffuses and changes the resist chemistry.
  4. Develop: the exposed (positive tone) resist dissolves; the pattern is left in resist.
  5. Etch or implant: the resist protects what it covers, then it is stripped.

Scanners

SourceλNASingle-exposure pitchUsed for
KrF248 nm0.93≈ 180 nmnon-critical layers, implants
ArF immersion193 nm1.35≈ 76–80 nmcritical layers to 7 nm with multiple patterning
EUV13.5 nm0.33≈ 28–32 nm7, 5, 3 nm critical layers
High-NA EUV13.5 nm0.55≈ 16–20 nm2 nm and beyond

Terms

NA
Numerical aperture: how wide a cone of light the lens collects. Water immersion lifts it above 1.
k1
Process factor in half-pitch = k1·λ/NA. The physical limit for lines and spaces is 0.25.
σ (partial coherence)
Size of the illumination; off-axis shapes (annular, dipole) push resolution further.
DOF
Depth of focus: the focus range over which the CD stays in spec, ≈ λ/NA².
Bossung plot
Printed CD versus focus for several doses: the process window.
LELE
Litho-etch-litho-etch: two masks, interleaved; overlay error becomes CD and space error.
SADP / SAQP
Self-aligned double / quadruple patterning: spacers on mandrels halve or quarter the pitch.
Cut mask
Extra mask that removes unwanted parts of the regular lines made by spacer patterning.
OPC
Optical proximity correction: serifs, hammerheads and biases on the mask compensate rounding and shortening.
Stochastics
Random photon and acid counts in tiny features: rough edges, missing or merged contacts.
LCDU
Local CD uniformity: random variation of neighbouring features.

How it works

Explain the terms: Black's equation, Blech length, NBTI, HCI, TDDB, HTOL, FIT, Weibull, AEC-Q100

Wear-out mechanisms

MechanismWhereDriven byModel
ElectromigrationMetal lines, viasCurrent density, temperatureMTTF = A·J⁻ⁿ·e^(Ea/kT)
Stress migrationVias over wide metalTemperature, mechanical stressPeaks near 150–200 °C
NBTI / PBTIPMOS / NMOS gate stackGate voltage, temperatureΔVth ∝ t^0.15–0.25
HCINear the drainDrain voltage, switchingΔVth ∝ t^0.4–0.5
TDDBGate oxide, BEOL dielectricElectric field, temperatureWeibull, β ≈ 1–2

AEC-Q100 temperature grades

GradeAmbient rangeTypical use
0−40 … +150 °CEngine compartment
1−40 … +125 °CMost under-hood electronics
2−40 … +105 °CPassenger compartment hot spots
3−40 … +85 °CMost cabin electronics

Terms

Black's equation
Electromigration lifetime falls with current density squared and rises exponentially as temperature drops.
Blech length
Below a critical product of current density and length, back-stress stops the atom flow: short lines are immune.
NBTI
Negative bias temperature instability: interface traps raise the PMOS threshold over time.
HCI
Hot carrier injection: fast electrons near the drain damage the oxide interface.
TDDB
Time-dependent dielectric breakdown of the gate or inter-metal dielectric.
HTOL
High-temperature operating life test: parts run at 125 °C and raised voltage for 1000 h.
Acceleration factor
Hours of use that one test hour represents: Arrhenius for temperature, plus a voltage term.
FIT
Failures in time: failures per 10⁹ device-hours. 1 FIT ≈ one failure in 114 000 device-years.
Weibull β
Shape of the failure distribution: < 1 early failures, 1 random, > 1 wear-out.
AEC-Q100
Stress-test qualification for automotive ICs from the Automotive Electronics Council.

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: layout, GDS, mask layer, λ rules, standard cell, DRC, LVS, well tap

From layout to masks

  1. Draw: each layer of the layout is a set of polygons (the GDSII or OASIS file).
  2. Check: DRC checks every width, space and enclosure; LVS extracts the circuit and compares it with the schematic.
  3. Tape out: the checked layout goes to the mask shop, often after OPC.
  4. Masks: each layer becomes one or more photomasks, used in the process flow.

Layers of this cell

LayerBecomesProcess step
n-welln-type region for the PMOSWell implant
ActiveSilicon islands (everything else is STI)STI litho and etch
PolyGates and short wiresGate patterning
n+ / p+Source/drain dopingS/D implants
ContactTungsten plugs to active and polyContact etch and fill
Metal 1First copper wiring, VDD and VSS railsM1 damascene

Terms

Layout
The top-view drawing of every layer of a chip; a transistor is where poly crosses active.
GDSII / OASIS
File formats that hold the polygons of a layout.
λ rules
Scalable design rules: every width and space is a multiple of λ, half the minimum gate length.
Standard cell
A small fixed-height layout (inverter, NAND, flip-flop) with VDD and VSS rails at the top and bottom, so cells abut in rows.
Poly endcap
Extension of the gate beyond the active area, so the gate still cuts the channel if the masks are slightly misaligned.
DRC
Design-rule check: thousands of geometric rules that keep the layout manufacturable.
LVS
Layout versus schematic: the extracted devices and connections must match the circuit.
Well tap
Contacts that tie the n-well to VDD and the substrate to VSS, against latch-up.
RD

Range-Doppler processing

Controls

FFT window
Chirps per frame
Noise per sample
Range cut through
Guard cells
Training cells
False-alarm probability
Virtual channels
Angle between two cars

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: data cube, range FFT, Doppler FFT, CFAR, angle FFT, point cloud

One radar frame, step by step

  1. Chirps: the transmitter sends a burst of fast chirps; each echo is mixed down to a beat signal and sampled by the ADC.
  2. Range FFT: the beat frequency of each target becomes a peak at its range bin.
  3. Doppler FFT: across chirps, the phase of each range bin rotates with the target's speed.
  4. CFAR: an adaptive threshold separates targets from noise and clutter.
  5. Angle FFT: across the virtual antenna channels, the phase step gives the direction.
  6. Point cloud and tracking: detections with range, speed and angle feed the tracker and the sensor fusion.

This radar

ParameterValue
Carrier77 GHz (λ = 3.9 mm)
Range resolution0.5 m (B = 300 MHz)
Samples per chirp128 (range up to 64 m)
Chirp repetition50 µs (±19.5 m/s unambiguous)
Virtual channels4–64 at λ/2 spacing

Terms

Data cube
Samples × chirps × channels of one frame; the three FFTs run along its three axes.
Range bin
One output of the range FFT: a slice of distance ΔR = c/2B wide.
Doppler bin
One output of the Doppler FFT: a slice of radial speed.
Window
Taper applied before an FFT to lower sidelobes, at the cost of resolution.
CFAR
Constant false-alarm rate: the threshold follows the local noise so the false-alarm rate stays fixed.
Clutter
Echoes from things that are not targets: road, guardrails, buildings; mostly at zero speed.
Point cloud
The list of detections with range, speed, angle and amplitude for each frame.
Integration gain
Coherent FFTs over N samples raise the signal-to-noise ratio by 10·log10 N.

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: CD-SEM, OCD, overlay, control chart, Western Electric rules, Cpk, run-to-run control

From measurement to action

  1. Sample: a few wafers per lot and a few sites per wafer are measured after key steps.
  2. Measure: CD-SEM, scatterometry, overlay, film thickness and defect inspection.
  3. Chart: each result goes on a control chart with limits from the normal behaviour of the process.
  4. React: a rule violation holds the lot or the tool (out-of-control action plan).
  5. Correct: run-to-run controllers feed the measurements back into the next lot's recipe.

Typical inline measurements

ToolMeasuresPrecision (3σ)
CD-SEMLine width, roughness, contact size~0.2–0.5 nm
Scatterometry (OCD)Width, height, sidewall angle, profile~0.1–0.3 nm
Overlay (image or diffraction)Layer-to-layer alignment~0.2–0.5 nm
EllipsometryFilm thickness and optical constants~0.05 nm
Defect inspectionParticles and pattern defectssensitivity ~10–20 nm

Terms

CD
Critical dimension: the width of the smallest lines or holes of a layer.
LER / LWR
Line-edge and line-width roughness: the 3σ variation of an edge or of the width along a line.
Scatterometry
Optical CD: measure the spectrum reflected by a grating and find the profile whose simulated spectrum fits it.
Overlay
Misalignment between two patterned layers, corrected by the scanner per lot.
Control limits
±3σ of the process when it is stable; not the same as the specification limits.
Western Electric rules
Patterns on a control chart that are unlikely by chance and signal a change in the process.
Cp / Cpk
Process capability: how many 3σ fit between the mean and the nearest spec limit.
Run-to-run (R2R)
Feedback that adjusts the recipe of the next lot from the measurements of earlier lots.

Package thermal network

Controls

Cooling
Die-to-lid TIM
Workload

Ambient temperature
Die thickness
Throttle temperature
Peak power

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: junction temperature, θJA, θJC, TIM, heat spreading, hot spot, thermal impedance, throttling

Where the heat goes

  1. Transistors: switching and leakage turn almost all electrical power into heat in a thin layer at the top of the silicon.
  2. Die and TIM1: heat crosses the silicon and the thermal interface into the lid.
  3. Lid and TIM2: the copper lid spreads it out; a second interface couples it to the heat sink.
  4. Heat sink: fins, a fan or a liquid loop hand it to the air or the coolant.
  5. Board path: a smaller part flows down through the substrate, the solder balls and the board.

Typical thermal resistances

Partθ (°C/W)
Die and lid (θJC)0.05–0.3 for a large CPU
Thermal paste (TIM2)0.05–0.1
Tower heat sink with fan0.15–0.3
Liquid cold plate and radiator0.08–0.15
Phone SoC to ambient10–20

Terms

Junction temperature Tj
Temperature of the transistors; reliability and leakage depend on it, limits are 85–125 °C.
Thermal resistance θ
Temperature rise per watt of heat flow, in °C/W: the thermal version of Ohm's law.
θJA, θJC
Junction to ambient, junction to case: the standard package figures in a data sheet.
TIM
Thermal interface material: grease, solder or liquid metal that fills the gap between two surfaces.
Heat spreading
Sideways conduction in the silicon and the lid that lowers the peak temperature of small hot blocks.
Hot spot
A small block with high power density, much hotter than the die average.
Thermal impedance Zth(t)
Temperature rise after a power step, as a function of time; each layer adds a time constant τ = R·C.
Throttling
Lowering clock frequency and voltage when Tj reaches its limit, to stay safe.

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: Czochralski, segregation, epitaxy, SOI, conformality, ALD, anisotropy, ARDE, CMP, dishing, erosion

The four building blocks of every process flow

  1. Add: deposition grows films: oxidation, PVD, CVD, ALD, epitaxy, electroplating.
  2. Pattern: lithography defines where (see the Lithography tab).
  3. Remove: etch transfers the pattern; CMP flattens the surface.
  4. Modify: implantation and anneals change the doping and the crystal.

Deposition methods compared

MethodConformalityTypical use
PVD (sputtering)Poor, line of sightBarrier and seed layers, metal
CVDGood to fairOxide, nitride, tungsten, polysilicon
ALDNear perfectHigh-k gate oxide, spacers, liners
EpitaxyFollows the crystalStrained SiGe, S/D, epi wafers
ElectroplatingBottom-up fillCopper interconnect

Terms

Czochralski (CZ)
Growing a single-crystal ingot by slowly pulling a rotating seed out of molten silicon.
Segregation coefficient k₀
Ratio of dopant concentration in the crystal to that in the melt; below 1, the melt gets richer as the ingot grows.
Epitaxy
Growing a crystalline layer that continues the lattice of the substrate.
SOI
Silicon on insulator: a thin silicon layer on a buried oxide, made by Smart Cut (hydrogen implant, bond, split).
Conformality
How evenly a film covers the top, sidewalls and bottom of a feature; step coverage is bottom over top thickness.
ALD
Atomic layer deposition: alternating self-limiting surface reactions add one monolayer per cycle.
Anisotropy, ARDE
Etching straight down rather than sideways; aspect-ratio-dependent etching makes narrow features etch slower (RIE lag).
Dishing, erosion
CMP artefacts: wide metal lines sag in the middle, dense arrays lose oxide and metal together.

Local mismatch

Controls

Technology
Width W
Length L
Process corner
Supply voltage
Temperature
Array size
Cell supply
σVt of cell transistors

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: global and local variation, Pelgrom law, corners, PVT, Monte Carlo, SNM, sigma

Where variation comes from

  1. Wafer to wafer, lot to lot: tool drift, chamber differences: global shifts of all transistors.
  2. Across the wafer: thickness and dose gradients from centre to edge.
  3. Within the die: layout context, stress, density effects.
  4. Device to device: random dopants, line-edge roughness, metal-gate grains: pure chance, uncorrelated even for neighbours.

Typical sign-off corners

CheckWorst corner
Setup timing (too slow)SS, low V, hot or cold
Hold timing (too fast)FF, high V, cold
Leakage, powerFF, high V, hot
Analog offsetMonte Carlo of mismatch
SRAM stabilityFS / SF, low V, local 6σ

Terms

Global variation
Shifts every transistor on a die the same way; captured by process corners.
Local mismatch
Random differences between identical neighbouring transistors.
Pelgrom law
σ(ΔVt) = A_Vt / √(W·L): mismatch averages out over a larger area.
Process corner
A model file at about ±3σ of the global spread, such as SS or FF.
PVT
Process, voltage and temperature: the three axes of sign-off.
Monte Carlo
Simulating many random samples of the device parameters to get a distribution.
SNM
Static noise margin: how much noise an SRAM cell tolerates before it flips; the largest square in the butterfly curve.
Sigma
Mean over standard deviation of a margin; a gigabit memory needs more than 6σ per cell.

From RTL to GDS

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: RTL, synthesis, place and route, clock tree, STA, slack, sign-off, tape-out, DFT, scan, ATPG, DPPM

The digital flow in one line each

  1. RTL: the behaviour written in Verilog or VHDL, verified by simulation.
  2. Synthesis: RTL mapped to standard cells of the target library under timing constraints.
  3. Place and route: cells placed in rows, clock tree built, wires routed in the metal layers.
  4. Sign-off: static timing at all corners, power and IR drop, DRC and LVS.
  5. Tape-out: the GDS/OASIS file goes to the mask shop; first silicon follows months later.
  6. Test: scan patterns and memory BIST screen every die on the tester.

Typical numbers for a large SoC

ItemValue
Standard cells100 million – several billion
Flip-flops (scan cells)10–100 million
Timing paths checkedbillions, at dozens of corners
Masks at 3 nm~70–80
Automotive quality target< 1 DPPM

Terms

RTL
Register-transfer level: registers and the logic between them, described in a hardware language.
Standard cell
A pre-designed gate or flip-flop of fixed height from the foundry library.
Clock tree
Buffers and wires that deliver the clock to every flip-flop with small skew.
STA, slack
Static timing analysis checks every path; slack is the margin left before the deadline, negative means a violation.
Setup, hold
Data must arrive before the next clock edge (setup) and must not change too soon after it (hold).
DFT, scan
Design for test: flip-flops are chained into shift registers so a tester can set and read every state.
ATPG
Automatic test pattern generation: finds input patterns that expose each modelled fault.
DPPM
Defective parts per million that escape test and reach the customer.

Equations

Analysis

How it works

Explain the terms: SerDes, insertion loss, ISI, eye diagram, FFE, CTLE, DFE, PAM4, jitter, BER, UCIe

Inside a SerDes link

  1. Serializer: wide parallel data becomes one fast bit stream.
  2. TX driver + FFE: pre-distorts the symbols to fight the channel.
  3. Channel: package, board, connector, cable; loss grows with frequency.
  4. RX CTLE + DFE: boosts high frequencies and cancels the tail of earlier symbols.
  5. CDR and slicer: recovers the clock and decides each symbol.
  6. Deserializer + FEC: back to parallel data, errors corrected.

Typical links

LinkRate per laneEnergy
PCIe 6.064 GT/s PAM4~5 pJ/bit
Ethernet 224G LR224 Gb/s PAM4~5–7 pJ/bit
XSR die-to-die112 Gb/s~1.5 pJ/bit
UCIe advancedup to 32 GT/s~0.25 pJ/bit
HBM3 per pin6.4 Gb/s~3–4 pJ/bit

Terms

Insertion loss
Attenuation of the channel in dB; skin effect and dielectric loss make it grow with frequency.
ISI
Inter-symbol interference: each smeared pulse leaks into its neighbours.
Eye diagram
All symbol periods overlaid; the open area is the margin for the decision.
FFE, CTLE, DFE
Feed-forward, continuous-time linear and decision-feedback equalizers.
PAM4
Four amplitude levels, two bits per symbol, three eyes each a third as tall.
Jitter
Timing uncertainty of the edges: random (Gaussian) plus deterministic (bounded).
BER
Bit error ratio; 10⁻¹² before FEC is a classic target.
UCIe
Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express: a standard parallel die-to-die interface for chiplets.
